derivations.claim: Put $d=\mathbf1-C\mathbf1$. Telescoping gives $\mathbf1-C^n\mathbf1=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}C^k d$, since $(I-C)\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}C^k=I-C^n$. Each summand is coordinatewise nonnegative by [A1].

For each $i$, choose by [A2] a path of length $s_i\le n-1$ from $i$ to $r$. The product of the positive edge weights along it is a positive term of $(C^{s_i})_{ir}$; for $s_i=0$ this entry is $1$. Hence $(C^{s_i}d)_i\ge(C^{s_i})_{ir}d_r>0$. Step 1.1 then gives $(C^n\mathbf1)_i<1$ for every $i$.

Let $q:=\max_i(C^n\mathbf1)_i<1$. Since $C^s\mathbf1\le\mathbf1$ for $0\le s<n$, nonnegativity gives $C^{kn+s}\mathbf1\le q^k\mathbf1$ for all $k\ge0$ and $0\le s<n$. Therefore $\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}C^j\mathbf1$ converges coordinatewise and its sum $v$ satisfies $v\ge\mathbf1>0$.
Multiplying the convergent series by $C$ shifts its terms, so $Cv=v-\mathbf1<v$ coordinatewise.

citations.quote:
Let $F$ be either $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $n\ge1$, fix the coordinate
order $1,\ldots,n$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$. Define $D,L,U\in M_n(F)$
by

$$D_{ij}=\begin{cases}a_{ii}&i=j,\\0&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad L_{ij}=\begin{cases}-a_{ij}&i>j,\\0&i\le j,\end{cases}\qquad U_{ij}=\begin{cases}-a_{ij}&i<j,\\0&i\ge j.\end{cases}$$

Thus $D$ is diagonal, $L$ is strictly lower triangular, $U$ is strictly upper
triangular (in the sense of
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]), and
$A=D-L-U$. If $A=A^*$, then $U=L^*$, where $*$ denotes conjugate transpose.
The decomposition uses the fixed coordinate order and is an exact-arithmetic
identity.

Input $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$, and an
iteration budget $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Check dimensions; on a mismatch return
`invalid-input`. Form $D,L,U$ by
[[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]. If some diagonal entry of
$A$ is zero, return `pivot-failure(i)` for the least such index $i$.

Otherwise set $M=D$ and $N=L+U$, so $A=M-N$. For each
$k=0,\ldots,m-1$, compute the diagonal solve

$$D x^{(k+1)}=(L+U)x^{(k)}+b,$$

equivalently, simultaneously for every $i$,

$$x_i^{(k+1)}=\frac{b_i-\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}}.$$

Return `completed` with $x^{(m)}$. The solve is the unique diagonal instance of
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] when the pivot
check succeeds; [[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]]
gives its well-definedness. A zero budget returns $x^{(0)}$. The procedure
reports no convergence or accuracy certificate.

Input $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$, and an
iteration budget $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Use the fixed order $1,\ldots,n$. Check
dimensions; on a mismatch return `invalid-input`. Form $D,L,U$ by
[[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]. If some diagonal entry of
$A$ is zero, return `pivot-failure(i)` for the least such index $i$.

Otherwise set $M=D-L$ and $N=U$, so $A=M-N$. For each
$k=0,\ldots,m-1$, solve the lower-triangular system

$$ (D-L)x^{(k+1)}=Ux^{(k)}+b $$

by forward substitution in increasing index order. Equivalently, the component
updates are

$$x_i^{(k+1)}=\frac{b_i+\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}x_j^{(k+1)}+\sum_{j>i}U_{ij}x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.$$

Return `completed` with $x^{(m)}$. The lower-triangular solve is unique after
the pivot check by [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]]
and [[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]].
A zero budget returns $x^{(0)}$. The procedure reports no convergence or
accuracy certificate.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

1. If $L\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with nonzero diagonal, the forward
   substitution recursion of
   [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] produces the
   unique solution of $Lx=b$.
2. If $U\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, the backward
   substitution recursion produces the unique solution of $Ux=b$.

Each solve uses exactly $n$ divisions,
$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ multiplications, and $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ additions or
subtractions, hence $O(n^2)$ scalar operations.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ admit a **matrix splitting**

$$A=M-N,$$

where $M\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F)$ is invertible in the sense of
[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]. The associated
**stationary iteration** for the system $Ax=b$ is

$$x_{k+1}=M^{-1}Nx_k+M^{-1}b.$$

Its iteration matrix is

$$B:=M^{-1}N.$$

Let $A=M-N$ be a matrix splitting in $M_n(\mathbb C)$ with stationary iteration

$$x_{k+1}=M^{-1}Nx_k+M^{-1}b,$$

and let $B:=M^{-1}N$ be its iteration matrix. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. For every right-hand side $b$ and every initial vector $x_0$, the iterates
   converge to the unique solution of $Ax=b$.
2. The spectral radius $\rho(B)$ is strictly less than $1$.

derivations.claim: By [A1], every $a_{ii}\ne0$. Thus $D$ and the lower-triangular matrix $D-L$ have nonzero diagonal, so the solves in [F1] and [F2] are uniquely defined by [L2].
By [F1]–[F2] and [L3], the iteration matrices are $G_J=D^{-1}(L+U)$ and $G_G=(D-L)^{-1}U$.

For each row $i$, set $q_i=\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|/|a_{ii}|$ and $q_J=\max_i q_i<1$. Since $L_{ij}=-a_{ij}$ below the diagonal and $U_{ij}=-a_{ij}$ above it, $\sum_j|(G_J)_{ij}|=q_i$. Hence for any eigenpair $G_Jz=\lambda z$ with $z\ne0$, choose $i$ with $|z_i|=\max_j|z_j|$; the row equation gives $|\lambda||z_i|\le q_i|z_i|\le q_J|z_i|$, so $|\lambda|<1$ and $\rho(G_J)<1$.

Let $G_Gz=\lambda z$ with $z\ne0$, and choose $i$ with $|z_i|=\max_j|z_j|=:R$. The equation $Uz=\lambda(D-L)z$ in row $i$ is $\sum_{j>i}U_{ij}z_j=\lambda(a_{ii}z_i-\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}z_j)$, so $|\lambda|\,|a_{ii}z_i-\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}z_j| \le\sum_{j>i}|U_{ij}||z_j|$. By the reverse triangle inequality and [A1], the left factor is at least $|\lambda|(|a_{ii}|-\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|)R$, while the right side is at most $\sum_{j>i}|a_{ij}|R$. Therefore $|\lambda|\le\max_i\frac{\sum_{j>i}|a_{ij}|}{|a_{ii}|-\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|}<1$; the denominators are positive and each strict inequality follows from [A1]. Thus $\rho(G_G)<1$.
The bounds in steps 3.1 and 3.2 and [L4] imply that both methods converge to the unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every $b$ and every initial vector.

boundaries.reason: The theorem assumes n≥1.

boundaries.evidence: Strict row dominance forces |a_ii|>0 in every row, so no pivot failure occurs (step 1.1).
For n=1, strict dominance gives a_11≠0 and both iteration matrices are zero, so one update solves the system (steps 1.1–4.1).
For diagonal A with nonzero diagonal, both iteration matrices vanish and one update returns A^{-1}b (steps 2.1–4.1).
The strict inequality gives q_J<1 and q_G<1; equality rows are excluded and treated by the separate weak theorem (steps 3.1–3.2).
Only a finite maximum and an eigenvector for each eigenvalue are used; no arbitrary-index choice is needed (steps 3.1–3.2).

Let $n\ge1$ and let $C=(c_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ have nonnegative entries
and row sums at most $1$. Form the directed graph with vertices
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and an edge $i\to j$ exactly when $c_{ij}>0$; assume this
graph is strongly connected, with paths of length $0$ allowed. Assume one row
$r$ has sum strictly less than $1$. Then, with $\mathbf1=(1,\ldots,1)^T$,

$$C^n\mathbf1<\mathbf1$$

coordinatewise, and the series $v=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}C^k\mathbf1$ converges
coordinatewise to a vector satisfying $v>0$ and $Cv<v$ coordinatewise.

derivations.claim: If $n>1$ and $a_{ii}=0$, [A1] forces every off-diagonal entry in row $i$ to vanish, contradicting strong connectivity. If $n=1$, the strict-row hypothesis forces $|a_{11}|>0$. Hence every diagonal entry is nonzero, and the Jacobi and lower-triangular Gauss–Seidel solves are defined by [L5].

Define $C_{ii}=0$ and $C_{ij}=|a_{ij}|/|a_{ii}|$ for $i\ne j$. Its row sums are at most $1$, one is strictly below $1$, and its positive-entry graph is the graph in [A1]. By [L2], choose $v>0$ with $Cv<v$, and set $q_J=\max_i (Cv)_i/v_i<1$.

By [F1], $|G_J|=C$ entrywise. For $\|z\|_v:=\max_i |z_i|/v_i$, nonnegativity gives $|G_Jz|\le C|z|\le\|z\|_v Cv\le q_J\|z\|_v v$. Thus every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $G_J$ satisfies $|\lambda|\le q_J<1$, so $\rho(G_J)<1$.

Set $B_L=|D|^{-1}|L|$ and $B_U=|D|^{-1}|U|$. Then $C=B_L+B_U$, $B_L$ is strictly lower triangular, and $(I-B_L)^{-1}=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}B_L^r\ge I$. Thus $H:=(I-B_L)^{-1}B_U=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}B_L^rB_U\ge0$. Since $(I-B_L)v-B_Uv=(I-C)v>0$, multiplying by $(I-B_L)^{-1}\ge I$ gives $Hv<v$. Consequently $q_G:=\max_i(Hv)_i/v_i<1$.

Because $D-L=D(I-D^{-1}L)$ and $D^{-1}L$ is strictly lower triangular, $(D-L)^{-1}U=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}(D^{-1}L)^rD^{-1}U$. Entrywise absolute values obey $|XY|\le|X||Y|$, so $|G_G|\le H$. The same weighted-vector estimate as in step 3.1 yields $\|G_Gz\|_v\le q_G\|z\|_v$; hence $\rho(G_G)<1$.
By [L3]–[L4], the two spectral-radius bounds imply convergence to the unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every right-hand side and every initial vector.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

Let $T$ be an endomorphism of an $n$-dimensional vector space over $F$. If

$$\chi_T(x)=\prod_{i<n}(x-\lambda_i)$$

in $F[x]$, then $\det(T)=\prod_{i<n}\lambda_i$. Thus the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.
The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F1], $M_\omega$ is lower triangular with diagonal $a_{ii}/\omega\ne0$, hence invertible by [L5]. Also $A=M_\omega-N_\omega$ by [L1], so [L2] applies with iteration matrix $G_\omega$. The matrix $N_\omega$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $(\omega^{-1}-1)a_{ii}$. Thus [L6]–[L7] give $\det(M_\omega)=\omega^{-n}\prod_i a_{ii}$ and $\det(N_\omega)=(\omega^{-1}-1)^n\prod_i a_{ii}$. From $M_\omega G_\omega=N_\omega$ and multiplicativity, $\det(G_\omega)=\det(N_\omega)/\det(M_\omega)=(1-\omega)^n$.

For sufficiency, suppose $A$ is positive definite and $0<\omega<2$. Then $Q:=M_\omega+M_\omega^*-A=(2/\omega-1)D$ is positive definite. For an eigenpair $G_\omega v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, one has $\lambda\ne1$ since $Av=(1-\lambda)M_\omega v$ and $A$ is invertible. Put $a=v^*Av>0$. Then $v^*M_\omega v=a/(1-\lambda)$, so $v^*Qv=a\left(2\operatorname{Re}\frac{1}{1-\lambda}-1\right) =a\frac{1-|\lambda|^2}{|1-\lambda|^2}>0$. Therefore $|\lambda|<1$ for every eigenvalue and $\rho(G_\omega)<1$.

If SOR converges for every right-hand side and start, [L3] gives $\rho(G_\omega)<1$. By [L8]–[L9], $|\det(G_\omega)|=\prod_{j=1}^n|\lambda_j|\le\rho(G_\omega)^n<1$. Step 1.1 therefore gives $|1-\omega|<1$, which for real $\omega$ is equivalent to $0<\omega<2$.

Assume now that SOR converges for every right-hand side and start. Then $\rho(G_\omega)<1$ by [L3], so $1$ is not an eigenvalue of $G_\omega$ and $I-G_\omega$ is invertible. By [L2], $A=M_\omega(I-G_\omega)$ is invertible. For $b=0$, its unique solution is $x_*=0$. For arbitrary $e^{(0)}:=x^{(0)}$, set $e^{(k)}:=x^{(k)}-x_*=x^{(k)}$ and $\delta_k=e^{(k+1)}-e^{(k)}$. The homogeneous SOR recurrence gives $M_\omega e^{(k+1)}=N_\omega e^{(k)}$, hence $Ae^{(k)}+M_\omega\delta_k=0$. Expanding the Hermitian quadratic form gives $(e^{(k)})^*Ae^{(k)}-(e^{(k+1)})^*Ae^{(k+1)} =\delta_k^*(M_\omega+M_\omega^*-A)\delta_k =(2/\omega-1)\delta_k^*D\delta_k$. The last equality follows from [L1] and [F1].

By step 2.1, $c:=2/\omega-1>0$. Summing the identity in step 2.2 from $k=0$ to $N-1$ and taking $N\to\infty$ (the error tends to $0$ by the assumed convergence) gives $(e^{(0)})^*Ae^{(0)}=c\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_k^*D\delta_k$. Moreover $\delta_0\ne0$: otherwise step 2.2 implies $Ae^{(0)}=0$, contrary to invertibility of $A$. Since $D$ has positive diagonal, the first summand is strictly positive and all others are nonnegative. Thus $(e^{(0)})^*Ae^{(0)}>0$ for every nonzero $e^{(0)}$, so [L4] gives that $A$ is positive definite.
By [L3], $\rho(G_\omega)<1$ implies convergence to the unique solution for every right-hand side and every initial vector. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the reverse implication.

For n=1 and A=[a] with a>0, the scalar recurrence has factor 1−omega, so convergence from every start is exactly |1−omega|<1, or 0<omega<2 (step 1.1).
For diagonal positive A, L=U=0 and G=(1−omega)I, so the same interval follows from the scalar eigenvalue calculation in step 1.2.
At omega=0 the procedure is undefined. At omega=2, convergence would force |1−omega|<1 by the determinant argument in step 2.1, which is false; hence there is no all-start convergence.
The polynomial roots and eigenpairs are finite-dimensional, and only a finite eigenvalue product is used; no arbitrary-family choice is needed (steps 1.2 and 2.1).
Positive definiteness and 0<omega<2 give rho(G)<1 in step 1.2; [L3] then gives all-start convergence in step 4.1.
All-start convergence implies the interval and positive definiteness (steps 2.1–3.1).

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ admit a **matrix splitting**

$$A=M-N,$$

where $M\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F)$ is invertible in the sense of
[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]. The associated
**stationary iteration** for the system $Ax=b$ is

$$x_{k+1}=M^{-1}Nx_k+M^{-1}b.$$

Its iteration matrix is

$$B:=M^{-1}N.$$

Let $A=M-N$ be a matrix splitting in $M_n(\mathbb C)$ with stationary iteration

$$x_{k+1}=M^{-1}Nx_k+M^{-1}b,$$

and let $B:=M^{-1}N$ be its iteration matrix. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. For every right-hand side $b$ and every initial vector $x_0$, the iterates
   converge to the unique solution of $Ax=b$.
2. The spectral radius $\rho(B)$ is strictly less than $1$.

routine_steps.claim: The matrices satisfy $M-N=I_2=A$ and $M$ is invertible. By [F1], $G=M^{-1}N=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2)$, whose spectral radius is $2$. The unique solution for $b=0$ is $0$.

The recurrence is diagonal, so from $x^{(0)}=(0,1)^T$ it gives $x^{(k)}=(0,2^{-k})^T\to0$, while from $(1,0)^T$ it gives $x^{(k)}=(2^k,0)^T$ and does not converge. This directly exhibits both the missing-unstable-eigenspace case and the failure of the all-start condition [L1] because $\rho(G)=2$.

Input $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$, and an
iteration budget $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Check dimensions; on a mismatch return
`invalid-input`. Form $D,L,U$ by
[[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]. If some diagonal entry of
$A$ is zero, return `pivot-failure(i)` for the least such index $i$.

Otherwise set $M=D$ and $N=L+U$, so $A=M-N$. For each
$k=0,\ldots,m-1$, compute the diagonal solve

$$D x^{(k+1)}=(L+U)x^{(k)}+b,$$

equivalently, simultaneously for every $i$,

$$x_i^{(k+1)}=\frac{b_i-\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}}.$$

Return `completed` with $x^{(m)}$. The solve is the unique diagonal instance of
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] when the pivot
check succeeds; [[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]]
gives its well-definedness. A zero budget returns $x^{(0)}$. The procedure
reports no convergence or accuracy certificate.

Let $n\ge1$ and $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfy strict row diagonal
dominance:

$$|a_{ii}|>\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).$$

Then the Jacobi and fixed-order Gauss–Seidel iterations defined by
[[alg-jacobi-stationary-iteration]] and
[[alg-gauss-seidel-stationary-iteration]] converge in exact arithmetic to the
unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb R^n$.

routine_steps.claim: The row inequalities are $5>1$ and $4>1$. Direct multiplication gives $A(5/19,13/19)^T=(2,3)^T$, so the displayed vector is the exact solution.

By [F1], $G_J=-D^{-1}(A-D)=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1/5\\-1/4&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-1/20$. Thus $\rho(G_J)=1/\sqrt{20}<1$; [L1] gives convergence from every initial vector to the verified solution.

Input $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$, a real
relaxation parameter $\omega$, and an iteration budget $m\in\mathbb N_0$.
Check dimensions; on a mismatch return `invalid-input`. If $\omega=0$, return
`invalid-relaxation`. Form $D,L,U$ by
[[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]. If some diagonal entry of
$A$ is zero, return `pivot-failure(i)` for the least such index $i$.

Otherwise set

$$M_\omega=\omega^{-1}D-L,\qquad N_\omega=(\omega^{-1}-1)D+U,$$

so $A=M_\omega-N_\omega$. For each $k=0,\ldots,m-1$, solve

$$M_\omega x^{(k+1)}=N_\omega x^{(k)}+b$$

by forward substitution in increasing index order. The lower-triangular
coefficient matrix has diagonal entries $a_{ii}/\omega$, which are nonzero
after the checks. Return `completed` with $x^{(m)}$. The solve is unique by
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] and
[[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]].
A zero budget returns $x^{(0)}$. This procedure is defined for every real
$\omega\ne0$; it reports no convergence or accuracy certificate.

Let $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian with strictly positive
diagonal, and let $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$. Write
$A=D-L-L^*$ by [[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]], and define

$$M_\omega=\omega^{-1}D-L,\qquad N_\omega=(\omega^{-1}-1)D+L^*,\qquad G_\omega=M_\omega^{-1}N_\omega.$$

The SOR iteration is $x^{(k+1)}=G_\omega x^{(k)}+M_\omega^{-1}b$. It converges
to the unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$ if and
only if $A$ is positive definite (meaning $x^*Ax>0$ for every nonzero $x$)
and $0<\omega<2$.

Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

$$x^*Ax>0$$for every nonzero vector $x\in \mathbb C^n$. A **Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal** of $A$ is a factorisation$$A=LL^*,$$

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real
number.

The Hermitian terminology matches
[[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]], and the
triangular terminology matches
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]].

routine_steps.claim: For $z=(z_1,z_2)^T$, $z^*Az=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2+|z_1-z_2|^2$, so [L2] shows that $A$ is positive definite; its diagonal is positive and $0<3/2<2$.

Here $D=2I$, $L_{21}=1$, and $U=L^*$. By [F1], $M_\omega=\begin{pmatrix}4/3&0\\-1&4/3\end{pmatrix}$ and $N_\omega=\begin{pmatrix}-2/3&1\\0&-2/3\end{pmatrix}$, hence $G_\omega=M_\omega^{-1}N_\omega= \begin{pmatrix}-1/2&3/4\\-3/8&1/16\end{pmatrix}$. Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2+(7/16)\lambda+1/4$, whose roots are $(-7\pm i\sqrt{207})/32$ and have modulus $1/2$.
The hypotheses of [L1] hold by step 1.1, so SOR converges for every start; in particular the stated start converges to the solution $0$.
